newsitem.title: USA: American Airlines, pilots meet for contract talks.
newsitem.headline: American Airlines, pilots meet for contract talks.

text.p: Contract negotiations between American Airlines and its pilots continued throughout the weekend but both sides declined to comment on Sunday on the progress of the talks.
"Talks are still ongoing at this moment as far as we know," Jim Philpot, a spokesman for the pilots' union said late on Sunday.

The Presidential Emergency Board (PEB) is expected to submit a proposed settlement to President Bill Clinton on Monday. The pilots' union said the PEB had not indicated when its report would be made public.
The White House convened the PEB on Feb. 15 to try to resolve the dispute between the nation's second largest airline and its 9,300 pilots.
The president of the Allied Pilots Association previously said the union and American Airlines would try to reach an agreement before the PEB submitted its report to Clinton.

The pilots' union said they would not make any additional comments about the progress of the talks until Monday. The union said its board planned to meet in Washington on March 21 and 22 to discuss the PEB's proposed settlement.
American Airlines, a unit of AMR Corp, also declined to comment on the duration or progress of the weekend's session.
"The PEB has indicated it wants everyone to refrain from commenting," a spokeswoman for the airline said.
Labour experts speculated the PEB aimed to have tacit approval on a labour agreement from both sides before submitting a report to Clinton.
This weekend's meeting at an undisclosed location was the first time in a month the two sides have resumed contract negotiations.

Last month, fruitless negotiations resulted in a brief pilots' strike on Feb. 15 which ended after Clinton intervened. The president's decision to convene the emergency board meant the pilots had to return to work for 60 days.
During the first 30 days, the board was to gather information and make proposals for an agreement. The pilots then have another 30 days to decide whether to accept the agreement.

If they reject it, they are free to strike again, although Congress can pass a law to force them to return to work and accept the board's proposed contract or to go into binding arbitration with the airline.

One issue in dispute is wages, with the pilots seeking an 11 percent pay increase to cover the last three years when there were no increases and also the next four years. American offered 6.6 percent.

At issue also is whether the union's pilots, who earn an average of $120,000 a year, will fly the new, small commuter jets American is to buy for its regional airline American Eagle, or whether they will be flown by Eagle pilots, who earn substantially less.
